articleTitle: A Three-Step Approach to Shift from Assessment Integrity to Assurance of Learning in the Age of AI
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: Maintaining academic integrity has become a challenge in engineering education with the increase in the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) by students. Combined with the lack of self-regulation skills in students, which are essential for workplace success, this issue highlights the need to rethink assessment design across programs of study. In this study, a mapping exercise evaluating current assessment practices across an academic program was carried out. Based on the learnings from this exercise, this paper proposes a three-step approach that shifts the focus from preserving assessment integrity to ensuring assurance of learning, whilst also addressing the limited opportunities universities offer for developing self-regulation through assessment. By embedding Assessment for Learning (AfL) principles throughout the curriculum, this approach offers the potential to foster deep learning, reduce the risk of AI misuse, and ensure students graduate as well-rounded, competent professionals in an AI-driven world.

articleTitle: Integral Evaluation For Engineering Graduates: Comparison Of Competency-based Assessment Tools
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: The transformation of competency-based education has laid new challenges for the evaluation systems of our students. In Mexico, there are several different types of evaluation that are used to assess the competencies required for graduation. One of the requirements to graduate at our institution is the application of the EGEL standardized exam, which is an instrument designed to evaluate knowledge and skills, both disciplinary and transversal, that we believe are essential for higher education graduates.Furthermore, there are other complementary evaluations that may allow the validation of the graduation competencies proposed in the different study programs of engineering students. In this regard, assessments can provide greater clarity about the strengths, abilities, and areas of improvement of the graduate candidates. They can help to evaluate the student’s analytical capacity, as well as their ability to collaborate and interact with other people, their orientation to detail as well as its results-based orientation. The aim of this article is to demonstrate the importance of applying integrated evaluations to students and to compare the results of standardized exams with the application of an integrative project assessment in B.S. in Computer Science and Technology program. The results obtained in the EGEL indicate levels of performance that can range from outstanding, satisfactory, or unsatisfactory. The results obtained indicate a high level of compliance, at least satisfactory. On the other hand, the results of the assessment of the integrative projects of the final year record the evaluation of the competences achieved at the sole level of the generation of students analyzed.

articleTitle: Enhancing Student Competency and Satisfaction through Assessment Modifications
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: This study explores the potential to enhance student competency and course satisfaction ratings by modifying assessment methodologies. Critical thinking skills, which are essential for analysing, evaluating, and synthesising information to solve complex engineering problems, are often underdeveloped in students. This underdevelopment is largely due to traditional assessments that tend to prioritise logical thinking over practical problem-solving. As a result, this hinders students from achieving higher-order competencies. Recognising the need for a more comprehensive evaluation system that prepares students for real-life engineering challenges, this study evaluated the transition from traditional to contemporary assessment methods in two non-numerical mining engineering courses between 2021 and 2023. The investigation aimed to identify factors contributing to student satisfaction during this transition, with a particular focus on feedback mechanisms, opportunities to demonstrate understanding, autonomous learning, and collaborative environments. The findings underscore the importance of these elements in assessment design, suggesting that they can enhance the holistic student experience while simultaneously improving competency.

articleTitle: Integrating Large Language Models into Engineering Education: Redesigning Peer Feedback Assessments for Enhanced Learning Outcomes
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: The widespread adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) in academic settings has raised concerns about student cheating and assessment integrity. While many educators respond by attempting to exclude LLMs from the learning process, this paper presents an alternative approach. We describe the redesign of a peer feedback assessment that was initially vulnerable to LLM-assisted cheating in an Engineering Education subject. Instead of resisting LLM use, we developed a new assessment that assumes student access to LLMs, focusing on skills that remain crucial in this context: selecting important feedback, delivering it effectively, and fostering generative conversations.This paper outlines the original task, its vulnerabilities, and the rationale behind the redesigned assessment. We present data from a pilot implementation, including student perceptions of the new process and its impact on their learning. The redesign aimed to enhance peer-to-peer learning, emotional connections, and support among students while potentially reducing marking costs. Our findings suggest that while the new approach presents some challenges, it offers significant benefits in terms of skill development, particularly in communication, empathy, and the task being fed back.We discuss the implications of this assessment redesign for student learning, including the potential trade-offs between leveraging LLMs for novel learning experiences and the development of critical thinking skills. This study contributes to the ongoing discourse on adapting engineering education to technological advancements, offering insights into innovative assessment strategies that embrace, rather than resist, the integration of AI tools in the learning process.

articleTitle: Romance Languages Plus Engineering Dual-Degree Programs: Increasing the Number of Women in Engineering?
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: Females are often underrepresented in engineering academic programs and the profession. This paper presents a strategy to address this issue. Female engineering students at the University of Georgia tend to minor in Romance languages more than their male counterparts. This trend suggests that female students are drawn to the combination of engineering and Romance languages. In response to this finding, the University of Georgia is developing an Engineering/Romance languages dual-degree program to improve the gender imbalance in the engineering field. If successful, this program could serve as a model for other universities seeking to address gender disparities in STEM fields. This study has significant implications for the future of engineering education, highlighting the need for greater diversity and inclusivity in STEM fields. By creating more appealing programs to a broader range of students, universities can help ensure that the next generation of engineers is more representative of the population. Numerous studies suggest a clear need for universities to address gender imbalances in STEM fields, and programs like Engineering plus Romance languages could be an effective way to do so. By providing students with a unique and valuable skill set, these programs could help attract more women to engineering and other STEM fields, ultimately leading to a more diverse and innovative workforce.

articleTitle: Microbe Detectives VS ChatGPT: Who Solves Better
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: This study examines ChatGPT, an Artificial Intelligence (AI) tool, to enhance learning and assessment in educational settings. The core of the research is the "Microbe Detectives" activity, where students use biochemical tests to identify microorganisms and then use ChatGPT to validate their findings. This approach is designed to improve students' laboratory skills and promote the ethical and responsible use of AI. The study includes a survey to evaluate the usability, cost, response quality, and overall student satisfaction with ChatGPT. The results indicate that although only 25% of students accurately identified the microorganism using only biochemical tests, the majority found ChatGPT helpful in exploring different outcomes and strengthening their conclusions. While some students expressed dissatisfaction with the accuracy of ChatGPT's responses, most appreciated the integration of AI into their learning activities. The study emphasises the importance of developing AI systems prioritising fairness, transparency, and accountability to build trust in their educational application. It also highlights the need for comprehensive training for educators and students to ensure the responsible and effective use of AI tools.

articleTitle: Industry-Driven Approaches to Teaching Waste Management: Designing Effective Educational Activities
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: This article examines the integration of industry-driven activities within undergraduate and postgraduate waste management courses. The study underscores the value of practical educational activities that incorporate both real-world examples and industry-standard approaches to enhance student comprehension and engagement in real-world waste management challenges. The "industry-driven" approach in this context refers to the use of learning activities based on real-world industry examples and the application of the waste management hierarchy as a structured framework for problem-solving. By incorporating these elements, the curriculum aims to equip students with critical thinking skills necessary for identifying waste reduction opportunities, prioritizing sustainable strategies, and effectively addressing waste management issues. The methodology includes implementing online games, assignments, and practical activities into Solid and Hazardous Waste Management courses, with data on student participation and assessment outcomes collected over three years. The observations suggest increased student interest and a deeper understanding of waste management concepts, indicating that such industry-driven approaches significantly enhance both theoretical knowledge and practical skill development essential for tackling real-world waste management issues.

articleTitle: Integrating alternative credentials to enhance academic experiences in engineering students
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: Continuous engineering courses commonly take place after the students graduate from higher education institutions. However, there is a gap between the skills required by the industry and the skills set provided throughout engineering courses. For this reason, both higher education institutions and industrial organizations, started questioning whether universities should have a bigger role in providing ready-to-work engineers, by assuring that the right skills are implemented in higher education programs. Moreover, continuous engineering education is an important strategy to promote engagement in higher education students as well as to strengthen their professional development. In this context, the innovative integration of a collaboration with the Mexican Ministry of Health (Secretaria de Salud) department was implemented in the Introduction to Professional Development course from the Biotechnology Engineering program at Tecnologico de Monterrey. This collaboration consisted in a series of 4 different in person certifications in disciplinary topics. A survey at the end of the course was applied to the students to evaluate, in a ten-point scale, the course in different parameters such as methodology and learning activities, intellectual challenge level, and learning guidance. The obtained results were compared to a control course without the integration of the certification program. After the courses’ implementation, the methodology and learning activities increased from 8.52 to 9.76, the intellectual challenge level increased from 8.52 to 9.72, and the teacher’s learning guidance was increased from 9.04 to 9.79. In conclusion, the integration of alternative credentials in higher education courses, not only prepare better up-to-date professionals for industrial challenges, but increases the students’ satisfaction regarding their courses.

articleTitle: Nurturing Capacity for Complexity: Embedding Systems Engineering into Bachelors Degrees
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: There is an increasing global need for engineers to work in complex socio-technical contexts, utilise systems thinking, and collaborate across disciplines and with experts and lay audiences. Systems engineering is one area that requires these skills and mindsets for successful practice in complex contexts. However, many systems engineering programs are only available to postgraduates which limits education opportunities and hence the overall number of engineers capable of working in complex domains and systems.To prepare graduates for complex engineering domains and multi-disciplinary practice a new systems engineering core was designed and embedded as a spine in an undergraduate program with numerous discipline majors. The development process involved research, benchmarking, and curriculum design, followed by a roll-out over four years aligning with an incoming student cohort. Key features of the new program include an agreed institutional systems engineering process lifecycle, inclusion of multiple application domains aligned with industry practice to cut across discipline areas, and a team-teaching approach with dedicated education support roles and tutor engagement. Coherent and staged learning activities echoed across the suite of courses encourages continuous student learning.The finalised core replicates systems engineering practice by engaging students in multiple authentic projects from perspectives covering design, analysis, management, and operations. This has resulted in improved student experience and involvement, and greater partner engagement. This work demonstrates that systems engineering can be delivered at undergraduate level to nurture systems thinking and embracing complexity in graduates. Achieving this requires a program-level approach, dedicated staff expertise and resources, and the need to replicate systems engineering practice in the design and delivery of the program.

articleTitle: Revolutionising Antenna Engineering Education: Project-Based Learning for Industry Demands
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: This study examines the impact of project-based learning (PBL) strategies in an antenna engineering course, with an emphasis on fabrication and experimental validation. Additionally, the antennas taught in the course are in the D- band frequency range (110 GHz to 170 GHz), relevant for 6G communications. The shift to D-band frequencies, commonly used in industry, allowed students to directly link theoretical concepts with practical applications. Employing PBL methodologies, we assessed student engagement, interest, and comprehension. Feedback indicated increased confidence and enthusiasm in designing new antennas. This approach not only enhances understanding but also prepares students for industry challenges.

articleTitle: Integration of Global Perspectives in Engineering Projects: A Systematic Literature Review on Students' Cultural Awareness, Communication Skills, and Adaptability
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: The integration of global perspectives in engineering projects is essential for preparing students to thrive in a highly interconnected and culturally diverse professional landscape. This systematic literature review examines the impact of global engagement on engineering students' cultural awareness, communication skills, and adaptability. Utilizing a systematic search and review methodology, we considered databases such as ScienceDirect, IEEE Xplore, Web of Science, Elsevier, and Google Scholar. Keywords including engineering education, global perspectives, international collaboration, cultural awareness, cross-cultural communication, adaptability skills, project-based learning, and interdisciplinary projects were employed to identify relevant literature. Both peer-reviewed conference proceedings publications and credible journal articles from 2010 to 2024 were preferred. Through this comprehensive approach, key pedagogical strategies and programmatic elements that enhance these competencies were identified. Findings indicate that international collaborations, culturally diverse team projects, and immersive global experiences significantly contribute to students' ability to navigate cross-cultural interactions effectively. Enhanced cultural awareness fosters inclusivity and ethical considerations in engineering practices, while improved communication skills facilitate clearer and more efficient information exchange. Additionally, adaptability is shown to be crucial in responding to dynamic global challenges. This review underscores the importance of embedding global perspectives in engineering education to cultivate well-rounded professionals equipped to address complex global issues. Future research directions and practical recommendations for curriculum design are also discussed to further support the development of these essential skills in engineering students.

articleTitle: Exploring Digital Learning Pathways: Student Use of Online Information Resources and the Role of AI
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: Digital tools, including AI-driven resources, have revolutionized student learning by providing vast information resources online. This study surveys engineering students to understand how they manage their learning processes, solve doubts, and use resources like Google, YouTube, and AI-driven tools. It investigates how students identify useful information and their opinions on these resources. The purpose is to explore the effectiveness of digital tools in helping students find accurate information and to assess their impact on critical thinking and problem-solving abilities. A mixed-methods approach, combining quantitative surveys and qualitative interviews with 245 students from the Technical University of Valencia, was employed. Surveys focused on students’ use of digital tools, criteria for evaluating information, and their opinions. An experiment was conducted where students researched a specific topic online, followed by interviews for deeper insights. Results indicate a heavy reliance on search engines, video platforms, and AI tools for quick academic queries, leading to information overload and superficial understanding. AI tools help identify useful information quickly but risk reducing critical thinking and independent problemsolving. The study confirms that while AI tools and digital platforms provide valuable support, they can reduce opportunities for deeper learning. Educational institutions should balance AI integration with strategies promoting independent thinking and problem-solving skills. Future research should explore long-term impacts and methods to sustain student engagement.

articleTitle: Developing Sustainability Competencies in Engineering Students through Problem-Based Learning in Fluid Mechanics
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: Sustainability competencies encompass a broad range of skills, including systems thinking, interdisciplinary collaboration, and the application of scientific and technical knowledge to solve complex problems, which are required by future engineers to address contemporary challenges. Problem-Based Learning (PBL) is an educational approach that has shown to effectively develop these competencies by engaging students in real-world problems that require critical thinking, collaboration, and application of theoretical knowledge. This study investigates how PBL can develop sustainability competencies in engineering student by understanding the differences and similarities in competency development between students enrolled in a Fluid Mechanics course involving concepts of fluid transport, storage, and processing. students working on distinct problem scenarios. The research question focuses on identifying which problem scenarios better facilitate the development of sustainability competencies. A comparative case study approach is used to analyze the differences in competency development between two groups of junior-year Sustainable Development Engineering students. Group A designed a water pumping and distribution system for a small town, while Group B focused on a centrifugal compressor in a carbon dioxide heat pump system. Data were collected through observations, reflective writing, and analysis of students' final products. Preliminary results indicate that both problem scenarios effectively support the development of sustainability competencies, but with differences in the types and levels of competencies achieved. While Group A focuses on systems thinking and practical application of fluid mechanics principles, Group B demonstrates a deep understanding of theoretical principles and fluid mechanics role in decarbonization technologies. Feedback from students will also led to adjustments in instructional methods, enhancing the learning experience and optimizing the development of competencies. Both problem scenarios enable students to apply theoretical knowledge in practical challenges, fostering critical thinking, collaboration, and technical proficiency. Greater awareness and commitment to sustainability were observed among students, as they were actively involved in the process of refining their problem-solving approaches and understanding the broader implications of their work. PBL helps to develop sustainability competencies in engineering students.

articleTitle: Building Research Capacity in Engineering Education: Insights from a Faculty Development Program
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: The "One Academic – One Paper" (1A1P) program, launched at a private university in Latin America, is a professional development initiative designed to enhance faculty research skills in engineering education. By pairing novice faculty with experienced researchers, the program provides mentorship throughout the research process, from question formulation to publication. This four-year study evaluates the program’s effectiveness by analyzing conference papers indexed in Scopus to identify trends and research topics. The results show a significant increase in faculty engagement and a positive shift in participation willingness. While retention was initially a challenge, the program now enjoys consistent involvement, with a growing number of faculty members actively seeking participation. 41 conference papers have been published, addressing diverse topics such as gender perspectives in engineering education, educational management, active learning, and technology-enhanced teaching. The 1A1P program has substantially strengthened faculty research capabilities, fostering a culture of academic excellence and collaboration. As the program continues to evolve, it aims to expand its impact, ensuring sustained contributions to engineering education research and the ongoing professional development of faculty and the School of Engineering.

articleTitle: Enhancing Project-Based Learning in Engineering Disciplines Through Emerging Technologies: A Systematic Literature Review
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: Project-based learning (PBL) is a widely recognized pedagogical approach that fosters active learning and problem-solving skills among engineering students. Over the past few decades, PBL has brought a significant transformation in engineering education by becoming a core methodology for moving toward engineering programs that support student-centered learning. PBL has shifted the focus of engineering education from being teacher-centered to student-centered. Instead of simply imparting knowledge to students, PBL encourages students to engage in active, collaborative learning through real-world projects. In addition, PBL methods place a strong emphasis on practical skills development, as students work on projects that simulate real-world engineering problems. This helps to ensure that engineering graduates are equipped with the skills they need to succeed in the workforce.The study aims to investigate how emerging technologies could play a pivotal role in enhancing project-based learning (PBL) within the field of engineering. Emerging technologies such as Virtual Reality (VR), Augmented Reality (AR), Internet of Things (IoT), Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), Robotics, Automation, Collaborative Tools, and Cloud Computing can further enrich the PBL experiences.This literature review-based research examines the role of emerging technologies in enhancing PBL experiences within engineering education. By synthesizing research findings from various disciplines, including education, engineering, and technology, this review identifies key trends, challenges, and opportunities associated with integrating emerging technologies into PBL curricula. The review explores how technologies such as virtual reality, augmented reality, simulation tools, and collaborative platforms can enrich PBL environments by providing immersive, interactive, and engaging learning experiences. Additionally, it discusses strategies for effectively incorporating these technologies into engineering courses, addressing issues related to accessibility, affordability, and pedagogical alignment.Through an analysis of empirical studies, theoretical frameworks, and best practices, this review offers insights into the potential benefits of leveraging emerging technologies to optimize PBL implementation in engineering education. Moreover, it highlights the need for further research to explore the long-term impact and scalability of these technological interventions in enhancing student learning outcomes, fostering innovation, and preparing future engineers for real-world challenges.

articleTitle: Strategies for Integrating Peace Engineering in Engineering Teaching and Learning
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: The world is experiencing unprecedented incidents of business failures, corruption, greenwashing and social and environmental damage caused by business, including in the Engineering sector. The role of Engineering Education is therefore no longer limited to teaching technical knowledge, skills and values, but also includes the social sciences and humanities intelligences to cope with the complex world within which Engineering work exists and the externalities of such work. This study investigates opportunities, challenges and models for integration of Peace Engineering into Engineering standardization, programme design, curricula design, pedagogies and assessment, as well as evaluation of resulting Graduate Attributes. The aim is to develop models for integrating Peace Engineering and metrics for measuring students’ aspirations towards Peace Engineering. The focus of this study prioritized developing countries. A systematic review methodology was adopted to identify opportunities, challenges and models for the integration of Peace Engineering into Engineering Education. The context of developing countries was be integrated into the literature analysis and development of possible models. We also develop metrics to measure graduates’ aspirations for Peace Engineering. We found that the conception of Peace is complex and often partially treated in different papers. Furthermore, Engineering Graduate Attributes articulated by accreditation bodies need improvement in wording to cater for Peace Engineering. Strategies for integration of Peace across all levels of educational development were also reviewed.

articleTitle: Profiling First-year Students: An Interdisciplinary Challenge for Curriculum Design and Accompaniment Strategies
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: The first-year transition is essential for student retention and success in higher education. This transition involves lifestyle changes, managing academic requirements, experiencing new situations, building networks with peers, and enhancing competencies for the learning process. In this context, it is important to design and develop strategies for student accompaniment to facilitate the adaptation process and strengthen their technical skills according to their discipline.Designing strategies to meet students’ needs means recognizing their entry-level status. In assessing competencies’ performance and attitudes towards the learning process it is crucial to use standardized instruments to collect accurate information for mapping a set of actions to support students’ academic experiences.Based on this, the School of Engineering at the Pontificia Universidad Javeriana has implemented a strategy for the first-year transition focused on profiling students’ competencies and attitudes toward mathematics and science. The instruments considered the PISA framework and other validated scales.Since 2021, instruments for assessing mathematical competencies and attitudes have been applied to approximately 2100 first-year students. The instruments conducted for science have been completed by around 600 first-year students in the second term of 2023 and the first term of 2024. Adjustments have been included in line with the obtained results during the instruments' application.A first approach to the data gives guidance on the strengths and difficulties in mathematics and science areas. Most students need to build up interest, motivation, self-efficacy, and self-concept. Furthermore, students require reinforcement of numerical and geometry knowledge, problem-solving and representation competencies as well as explaining scientific phenomena.Considering the exploratory results, a challenge has been declared for different departments and units at the university in the curriculum design process and the accompaniment strategies. To cope with this challenge, a committee with representatives from academic and non-academic units has been set up to discuss students’ entry-level characteristics and needs, and pedagogical strategies used in the teaching process.

articleTitle: Examining the Relationships between Online Approaches to Teaching and Learning based on Engineering Student Experiences
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: The use of online virtual teaching platforms enables educators to transition between face-to-face and online Teaching and Learning (T&L). Recently, traditional contact-based institutions adapted to accommodate T&L online, allowing exploration of different T&L environments (both in person and online) and approaches to instruction within these environments.Online classes can take place in three primary ways: virtual classes, pre-recorded sessions, or a combination thereof. These three modes of instruction promote the implementation of a flipped classroom and encourage the use of continuous assessments.This study examines student perceptions of the online T&L approach that renders the implementation of a flipped classroom and continuous assessment. These have increasingly been adopted by lecturers and facilitators in an engineering degree programme to accommodate the different learning environments and complement learning. Additionally, this study investigates student perceptions of the benefit of a five-year extended engineering degree designed to provide academic support and develop professional competencies in students. This study spans two years and lies parallel to a second paper that examines overall student perceptions of the different T&L environments in person and online, as well as the different T&L modes used to accommodate student learning online.A questionnaire consisting of closed- and open-ended questions was distributed to the 2021 and 2022 first- and second-year five-year engineering degree programme cohorts at the University of Pretoria. A quantitative data analysis of the closed-ended responses was conducted through ANOVA correlation tests.Results indicate that students do not perceive the benefits of a flipped classroom approach in the learning environments investigated, and the reasons for this vary from poor implementation from the lecturer/facilitator side to an inability to self-regulate one’s learning from a student’s side. Furthermore, there is an overwhelming preference for continuous assessment across all environments, as it highlights areas for development and encourages consistent reinforcement of content.

articleTitle: Empowering Engineering Students for the Energy Transition Via A Project-Based Learning Initiative in Collaboration with Industry Experts
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: The global energy transition presents significant challenges for engineering education, necessitating innovative approaches to prepare students for evolving industry demands. This paper presents a novel initiative implemented within the Unit Operations course at Sultan Qaboos University's Department of Petroleum and Chemical Engineering. The study aimed to enhance students' practical skills and industry readiness through an integrated approach combining project-based learning (PBL) and industry collaboration. The initiative centered on a semester-long project where students engaged in the detailed design of an absorption column for CO2 capture, guided by an industry expert with extensive experience in natural gas processing. The project was structured into four progressive memos, each building upon previous learning and aligned with course material. Results demonstrate significant improvements in student outcomes. Quantitative analysis revealed a 15% improvement in grade distribution and a 25% increase in engagement levels compared to previous cohorts. Qualitative feedback indicated enhanced problem-solving skills, improved understanding of industry practices, and increased confidence in applying theoretical knowledge to real-world scenarios. The industry expert's involvement ensured project relevance and provided students with valuable insights into professional practices. This study contributes to the discourse on engineering education by providing a practical framework for integrating PBL, industry collaboration, and sustainability considerations. The findings suggest that this approach effectively bridges the gap between academic learning and industry application, better preparing engineering students for the challenges of the energy transition. Future research could explore this model's long-term impact and transferability to different educational contexts and disciplines.

articleTitle: Adapting Studio-Based Learning in Engineering to Incorporate International Perspectives
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: This paper explores the integration of an international dimension into Australian engineering studio-based subjects through a strategic partnership with a French engineering school in Paris. The study uses an action research methodology to explore what worked successfully and to identify areas for future improvement, to guide others who seek to build international collaboration into engineering education programs. The program involved adapting a traditional engineering studio subject into a condensed 3-week accelerated format, as well as encouraging students to engage in enriching extracurricular activities and conversational French lessons. The challenges and opportunities encountered during 2 consecutive implementations of this novel subject in 2023 and 2024 are discussed, drawing insights from both students and academic teaching staff using feedback from participants and staff observations. This paper underscores the transformative potential of studio-based learning when conducted across geographical borders.

articleTitle: The New Engineering Education to Face Industry 5.0 Challenges
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: The shift from Industry 4.0 to Industry 5.0 indicates a human-centered, sustainable, and resilient workplace, emphasizing the integration of human factors into industrial systems and work processes. This paper examines how universities must redesign engineering programs to prepare students for the Industry 5.0 era, integrating advanced technologies with human-centric skills. The methodology involved a non-systematic mapping of literature and a cross-case synthesis of the main initiatives of ten universities in the United States, Latin America, and Europe, focusing on successful practices in engineering education. Two primary research clusters were identified: Industry 5.0 Challenges and Sustainable Socio-Economic Development. Findings suggest that universities with innovative, interdisciplinary engineering programs supported by global higher education associations are better positioned to meet Industry 5.0 requirements. This study underscores the importance of an interdisciplinary and holistic approach to engineering education, which is essential for addressing the complex demands of Industry 5.0.

articleTitle: Analysis of the Effect of Using AI as a Tool to Assist Mechatronics Engineering Students in Learning
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has revolutionized numerous aspects of our daily lives, and higher education is no exception. As AI technology continues to evolve, it becomes imperative to explore novel avenues through which it can enhance student training and bolster motivation and learning outcomes. This study aims to demonstrate the dedication and enthusiasm displayed by a cohort of Mechatronics Engineering students who utilized an AI bot to study classical control theory. The study objective was to illustrate that AI can be a valuable asset for educators when appropriately directed and trained. Furthermore, it aimed to showcase the influence of employing an AI bot on student motivation and learning outcomes. Although the results did not meet expectations concerning motivation to use the AI bot, the students’ learning outcomes were slightly better compared to the group that did not use the AI bot. To obtain comparative results, surveys were used to collect information from students.

articleTitle: Immersive Simulation for Digital Transformation Undergraduates: Exploring How to Enhance Soft Skills and Real-World Readiness in Agile Contexts
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: The Digital Transformation (DT) landscape demands new methodologies to improve project management outcomes. With many projects failing, Agile frameworks have become crucial for responding to changing customer demands. Managing Agile projects requires a deeper understanding and practical application of these principles. This paper shares experiences of using immersive gamification to teach Agile best practices in project management focusing on soft skills development. The goal was to bridge the theory-practice gap for engineering students, enhancing their Agile knowledge and practical-softt skills for lifelong careers. The research question was: How can we educate engineers to translate theoretical Agile into practical application in dynamic DT project management environments? The study employed the "Egypt Challenge Simulator," an immersive gamification tool applied to 36 engineering students. The activity allowed students to experience Agile practices and understand Scrum process, improve soft skills like project management, collaboration, and leadership, and recognize the real-world role of engineers in project management. The results suggest that hands-on Agile training, like the "Egypt Challenge Simulator," is crucial for bridging the theory-practice gap in project management. Evidence suggests that immersive gamification interactive training effectively prepares engineering students, enhancing their interpersonal skills, understanding of real-world roles, and improving their readiness in Agile contexts. A bivariate correlation analysis was conducted to explore the relationship between soft skills and real-world readiness in agile contexts. Based on eight identified categories, bivariate correlation suggests significant correlations between: social experience and effectiveness and engagement; effectiveness and engagement and satisfaction and application; knowledge acquisition and effectiveness and engagement; and social experience and satisfaction and application. These findings indicate that a comprehensive application of immersive gamified activities can generate a diverse, captivating, and fulfilling learning experience, enhance educational results, and develop soft skills by incorporating social, playful, guidance, and information acquisition elements.

articleTitle: Exploring the Capabilities and Limitations of Generative AI in Providing Feedback on Engineering Drawings: A Case Study
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: This paper explores and evaluates the use of OpenAI’s ChatGPT-4o as a feedback tool for engineering drawings. The AI feedback tool was trained on a synthetic dataset specifically created for the task, which included a comprehensive checklist derived from the Australian Standard for Technical Drawings (AS 1100) and a variety of engineering drawing examples. The evaluation involved repeated testing of three distinct case studies, each representing different levels of drawing accuracy. The findings reveal both strengths and weaknesses in the AI feedback tool’s performance, providing valuable insights into the capabilities and limitations of AI in providing feedback on engineering drawings in the education context. The research also highlights the need for further training to improve accuracy in certain areas and the potential bias in the evaluation process. A key observation from this study is that while Open AI’s ChatGPT-4o model can generate feedback, it may not truly ‘understand’ the engineering drawings in the same way a human would. This work contributes to the ongoing efforts to leverage AI in education, particularly in the context of engineering drawing feedback, and underscores the importance of human oversight and intervention in the application of AI technology.

articleTitle: Engineering as a Social Profession
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: This paper examines the social properties of the purpose and practices of engineering to develop a social ontology of the profession. Its social elements are considered in terms of its engagement with society (its social purpose), and in regard to the engineer’s engagement with the profession (the lived professional experience). Both aspects are important for the development of a social narrative. The social purpose of the profession has been explored by others, facilitating a review of the literature for this paper. The lived professional experience draws on autoethnographic observations of a curated, operational, engineering management system employed in daily professional practice, which in turn draws upon the accumulated experiences of many other professionals over lengthy periods of time. This is believed to be new for ethnographic studies of engineering practice. The findings collectively paint a comprehensive picture of engineering as a profession where social orientation is paramount, and the social skills of negotiation and collaboration are indispensable. The continuing gap between public perceptions and reality are a source of concern, especially when these perceptions may follow graduates into their early career experiences. Some factors that contribute to that gap are identified. For education, the study identifies the need for the curriculum to develop negotiation and collaboration skills.

articleTitle: Examining the Impact of Industry Partnerships on Project-Based Learning Initiatives within Engineering Education: A Systematic Literature Review
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: The emphasis on project-based learning (PBL) persists in enhancing engineering curriculum by giving students hands-on experience with real-world experiments, preparing them for the industry. Collaboration between academia and industry allows students to address actual industry challenges through PBL. This platform provides students with genuine learning experiences and industry practices that inspire them throughout their studies. It is important to highlight that South African institutions previously struggled to engage industry partners for educational purposes.The current systematic literature review study wishes to investigate the importance of industry partnerships on PBL within engineering education to benefit both students and industry demands.The systematic literature review methodology seemed appropriate for the current study due to its nature of extensively reviewing credible electronic databases. The electronic databases opted for included IEEE Xplore, ERIC, ScienceDirect, Web of Science, Elsevier, and Google Scholar. The keywords considered in this study included "project-based learning," "industry partnerships," and "engineering education." The inclusion and exclusion criteria focused on articles credible articles and peer-reviewed conference publications between 2010 and 2024.The industry partnership through PBL equips students with lifelong experiences coupled with problem-solving skills, critical thinking, teamwork, and professional competencies. Academics are also afforded opportunities for industry secondment where they spend some time in industry while being exposed to the latest technologies to enhance their teaching capabilities. The industry also grasps opportunities to co-own selected facilities by branding them.The findings of this systematic literature review highlight the importance of industry partnerships with institutions of higher learning through PBL initiatives. Students are also afforded opportunities to better understand the fundamentals of engineering principles in real life. The PBL platform allows students to do projects that bring real changes that they can see and feel. Industry is, therefore, able to comprehend that institutions of higher learning could provide much-needed solutions with their support.In the South African context, it is still a challenge to get the cooperation of industry to work with the institutions of learning regarding curriculum matters. As results engineering students even do their third-year Capstone design projects internally without the involvement of industry. It is therefore recommended that faculties should extend invitations to industry to bring their problems to be solved by students while supervised by academics.

articleTitle: Exploring Factors Influencing Dropout Among TVET College Students: A Relationship-Based Study
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: The National Certificate (Vocational) (NC(V)) programme was introduced in Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) colleges to enable college institutions to train and produce vocationally well-skilled artisans, who are anticipated to play a positive role in improving the nation’s economy. However, the programme has faced challenges of low levels of programme completion, high failure, and attrition rates since its inception and implementation. These low levels of completion, high failure, and attrition rates imply that the goal of training and producing vocationally skilled artisans is not being fully achieved. Therefore, it is crucial to pinpoint college experience factors that influence the likelihood of student dropout in TVET colleges and to explore the nature of the relationships these factors have with dropout likelihood. This study aimed to examine and identify the factors influencing the probability of dropout among NC(V) students in TVET colleges and to examine the nature of the relationships between these factors and students’ decision to dropout. Data were collected in four public TVET colleges located in Gauteng province, South Africa. From each college, one college campus offering NC(V) Engineering and Related Design (ERD) courses was selected to participate based on plausible approaches from expert recommendations using a Delphi approach involving management staff and corroborated by findings from an extensive literature review. The study employed a quantitative method to collect data on college students’ experiences and factors influencing dropout from students’ perspectives. The targeted population was NC(V) students enrolled in ERD programmes doing Levels 3 and 4. A sample of 169 NC(V) ERD students from four campuses was selected using purposive sampling from a population of approximately 600 students. Furthermore, one classroom at each level was selected using the quota sampling method. Data were analysed using the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS). The college experience factors that were found to have significant relationships with student dropout likelihood were: student self-motivation and missing classes, peer relationships, college support, and programme satisfaction. There is a need for TVET colleges to implement interventions that enhance student’s self-motivation and class attendance; encourage positive peer relationships and improve student satisfaction with the NC(V) ERD programmes.

articleTitle: Enhancing Engineering Education through DEI: A Pathway to Inclusive Future Practices
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: The article aims to address a wide range of topics to offer a complete and comprehensive vision of how diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) can strengthen education in this area of knowledge with a view to the future. A multifaceted approach is needed to promote diversity and equity in engineering, as highlighted by Colombian researchers in the context of Latin America. This includes addressing historical and institutional barriers, increasing representation, and creating inclusive organizational cultures. The authors further emphasize the importance of operational models and stakeholder involvement in creating a culture of equity and inclusion, as demonstrated in a private university in Mexico. Another author underscores the role of meaningful learning experiences, such as the Integrative Project strategy, in fostering values, transversal competencies, and disciplinary skills in systems engineering students. These strategies collectively contribute to a more inclusive and equitable engineering field, especially to DEI strategies.

articleTitle: Exploring Artificial Intelligence Utilization for Engineering Education and Research in Africa
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) holds immense potential to revolutionize engineering education and research in Africa, offering opportunities for innovation and sustainable development. This study aims to assess the current utilization of AI in African engineering education and provide recommendations for its enhancement, empowering African engineering students to lead in AI research efforts. Through a meticulously designed questionnaire, the researchers delved into various aspects of AI integration, including understanding and usage, ethical considerations, resource needs, learning methodologies, skills development, industry collaboration, and strategies for maintaining relevance in the AI era. The results indicate that while AI is actively used in Africa, its application often lacks depth. Therefore, there is a critical need to expand the use of AI for more engaging research applications, collaboration, and engineering practices. The insights gained from this research will help shape the future of engineering curriculum design to foster innovation and the global competitiveness of Africa. This pioneering exploration not only sheds light on the present AI landscape in engineering education and research in Africa but also ignites a vision for an AI-driven transformation that could position Africa as a leading contributor in engineering advancements on the global stage.

articleTitle: Scalable Community Mentorship: A Vision for Engineering Literacy & Access
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: Black and Hispanic/Latine communities remain underrepresented in engineering careers due to persistent economic, social justice, and human rights issues. Consequently, students from these communities face unique challenges when entering into engineering fields. Barriers s tem from economic disenfranchisement, racial profiling, lack of community, and an absence of cultural competence. However, many programs that aim to tackle these issues are not holistic nor scalable to the degree needed for broader impact. To address the lack of holistic and scalable mentorship programs for Black and Hispanic/Latine students, we analyzed AVELA - A Vision for Engineering Literacy & Access’ (AVELA) holistic student-led STEM engagement model. This model leverages multi-tier near-peer mentorship, mentor-embodied community representation, culturally responsive experiential & service-based learning, and compensated student-led community engagement. Thus far, AVELA has supported 361 university student instructors in teaching to 4,412 secondary school students across 213 classrooms. To evaluate members’ motivations for participating in this mentorship program, we conducted 24 semi-structured interviews with undergraduate and graduate AVELA members. We find AVELA’s holistic student-led STEM engagement model improves Black and Hispanic/Latine engineering students’ experience in post-secondary education. Reduced power dynamics, community involvement, soft skill development, as well as financial support and technical skill building were indicated as key motivators for students’ participation in the program. Students expressed that the depth, applicability, and scale of their mentorship relationships cultivated a reliable student community that empowered them to build a robust professional skill set.

articleTitle: Students as Partners: closing the gap between academic studies in engineering education and the first career
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: The CAREER Compass portfolios initiative was introduced to FEIT to achieve the cultural shift and create a community where students feel connected to the faculty and the engineering profession, personally accepted and respected. This project was run between September and November 2023 at UTS. Eight CAREER Compass Champions, one professional staff and two academics were involved in this project. Students learned how to navigate subjects to document their personal professional development, evidencing the enhancement of their professional skills over time. In this paper, the design process of the CAREER Compass portfolios initiative will be described. The authors will explain in what ways the CAREER Compass movement is closing the gap between academic studies and the real world of careers by helping students become more Collaborative, Agentic, Response-able, Engaged and Employment Ready (CAREER) graduates. The choice of each element and pedagogical practice applied in this project will be supported by literature and examples. At the same time, the designers of the project will share personal reflections on the design and delivery journey.

articleTitle: Catalyzing Sustainable Futures: Innovative Approaches in Capacity Building for the Community Engineering Response Team
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive capacity-building program designed for engineering students in Sudan, with a focus on fostering a Community Engineering Response Team (CERT). In response to a pressing scarcity of essential services in many communities, this initiative aims to equip engineering students with the knowledge and skills necessary to address local challenges and promote community self-reliance. The program is rooted in the ECHO model of All-Teach All-Learn, peace engineering principles, and the Sustainable Development Goals framework.Utilizing a virtual academic-community learning environment, Sudanese college students, young professionals, women and men of all ages, and youth were engaged in 18 biweekly sessions on solid waste management, along with an additional 5 sessions focused on design-centered entrepreneurship. These sessions, facilitated by national and international subject matter experts, employed a participatory approach and attracted approximately 700 participants from 11 engineering disciplines across 8 Sudanese universities in 6 different states.Post-program evaluations indicate significant knowledge enhancement, with 94.4% of participants reporting a heightened understanding of solid waste management benefits. A majority (78.7%) expressed a willingness to recommend the program, citing a balanced mix of lectures and interactivity (86.9%). Moreover, 74.7% intended to apply the acquired knowledge in their professional pursuits.Following the capacity-building phase, 40 participants progressed to the implementation stage, selecting projects aligned with community needs. These projects encompassed a community awareness program in rural areas, biogas, and compost production from organic waste, interlock production from plastic waste and sand, and Geographic Information System (GIS) mapping for solid waste. These engineers, who are actively engaged in the program, form the core of the Community Engineering Response Team (CERT), which is dedicated to addressing community challenges through sustainable engineering solutions.

articleTitle: Comparing Competencies Assessment Tools: Identifying the Most Effective and Accurate Approach
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: This paper presents a 3 years-long study that analyzes changes in student competencies assessment and performance, upon modification of assessment tools across different academic periods at a private Mexican university, focusing on their accuracy and reliability. In 2019, the university introduced a New Educational Model that is built on a student competency-based curricula; it uses active learning and considers Challenge Based Learning as the main learning technique for most courses. However, the assessment instrument that was selected at the time was a binary 'Observed or Not Observed' checklist, which led to an overly positive evaluation bias. After careful analysis, the university transitioned to a multi-level, competency-specific rubric designed by professors from various disciplines, allowing for a more granular evaluation.This study compares three full semesters of assessments using the original checklists (1730 students, 20 courses, 830 groups and 306 educators) and three semesters using the new rubrics (2856 students, 20 courses, 899 groups and 258 educators), utilizing a normalized assessment average. The comparison includes only those competencies assessed throughout the semesters starting from Spring 2020. .Analysis of the data (n=120,245 assessments) reveals that checklists generate a positive bias, resulting in a higher weighted average (92.9%) compared to rubrics (89.0%). This bias decreases with rubrics, bringing assessments closer to institutional goals. The data indicate a statistically significant difference (chi-square, p=1.35E-128) in assessment results provided by different instruments. As a result, the shift to rubrics appears to enhance professors and instructors’ evaluation of competencies across an array of courses, in turn providing students with a fairer performance and competency assessment, and educators with a more precise feedback tool. Further work is needed to include more students in the sample and implement more specific and improved rubrics.

articleTitle: You Are Not Alone! Collaborative Professional Development of the Engineering Educator Gaze
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: Developing holistic knowledge, skills, practices and values of engineering graduates for a supercomplex world has placed significant pressure on engineering educators, particularly those from under-resourced Global South contexts. A number of engineering educator capacity building initiatives in South Africa over the past two decades has led to the emergence of a community of practice, which is championing holistic engineering education initiatives. This paper analyses the professional development of a selected group of engineering academics who are active in scholarly informed education initiatives. Drawing on the reflective narratives in their teaching portfolios, Legitimation Code Theory is used to frame the development of a cultivated gaze, using the Sydney Model of Graduate Attributes dimensions of Self, Knowledge and World. The orientations to and relations between these dimensions enable a nuanced perspective on how engineering educators see themselves in their contexts. A key finding is the value of collaboration and community of practice. The paper hopes to contribute insights into how educators can be better supported to develop graduates with an ‘engineering for life’ ethos.

articleTitle: Addressing Challenges and Solutions for Scaling up Project-Based Learning Initiatives in Large Engineering Programs
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: Project-based learning (PBL) has become one of the preferred pedagogical approaches in engineering education to promote active learning, problem-solving skills, and real-world application of knowledge. It is seen as a platform to promote deeper learning of knowledge-in-use within engineering and science practices rather than memorizing material. Both educators and communities accepted PBL as an invigorating tactic to motivate students to learn. Additionally, PBL historically succeeded when academics modified the pace of instruction, scaffolded learning, and created differentiation. Educators can easily change their teaching practices when they comprehend the dynamics and importance of creating a conducive environment of teaching and learning.The current study proposes to address challenges for scaling up project-based learning initiatives in large engineering programs to prepare students to excel in their future careers and contribute meaningfully to society through a project-based learning approach to address the quality, relevance, and impact of engineering education.An intensive systematized literature review research methodology was conducted through renowned databases including Wiley, SAGE, Taylor and Francis, Elsevier, Springer IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar. The research study targeted peer-reviewed conferences and journal papers published between 2010 and 2024.The study findings highlighted the important role played by PBL in affording students an opportunity to put into practice their mastery of content coordinated the academics in preparation for their employability. It continues to challenge students to engage more in solving complicated content and they obtain critical thinking among others. In addition, fostering of PBL environment prepares engineering graduates for real-world challenges especially when factors such as curriculum design flexibility, supporting faculty readiness, investing in infrastructure, and refining assessment practices are considered irrespective of the size of the engineering projects. The findings further reveal various ways that academics, administrators, and policymakers could benefit from when implementing PBL in large engineering programs.

articleTitle: Engineering of the Future: The Influence of Educational Innovation
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: Educational innovation is a strategic initiative that universities have been integrating into their efforts for the continuous improvement of the teaching and learning process, and as a response to the demands of the environment and the profile of today’s students. The purpose of this research is to analyze cases of educational innovation to define a process of design, development, and implementation of innovative resources in engineering programs, which will facilitate other institutions that want to get involved in the use of technology for innovation in education. The research methodology is qualitative, using multiple case studies. The stages that were followed are: the definition of the cases of educational innovation with technology, description of 3 cases in engineering courses, comparative analysis of the cases and conclusions with a model using the process approach. The institutional strategy of educational innovation is integrated by the allocation of resources, constant training of teachers and staff with knowledge in educational technology, pedagogical advisors, and multidisciplinary work. The experience of design, development, and implementation of resources for educational innovation allows for the systematization of processes in each of the stages that lead to the successful completion of the innovative projects, that impacts to the learning experience of the student and the engineering of the future. Educational innovation supports competency-based education, which uses active learning as one of its fundamental elements, impacts on student engagement not only with their course but also with the discipline they are studying and facilitates the student’s learning process. Defining models that facilitate the educational innovation strategy helps to ensure the impact on the purpose of universities: the training of young people with life skills to transform our organizations and society into a better world.

articleTitle: Extended Reality in Information Systems Education - Analyzing Technology Readiness Levels
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: Extended Reality (XR) and its associated domains, Virtual (VR), Augmented (AR), and Mixed Reality (MR) technologies provide cutting-edge technological affordances in emerging learning environments. Information Systems Education (ISE) key activities are teaching and training. Teaching activities involve conceptual understanding whereas training activities consider practical applications and their implementation. To investigate the impact of XR in ISE, it is important to contextualize the Technology Readiness Level (TRL) of applications within the educational ecosystem. The progression from initial ideas (TRL-0) to full commercial applications (TRL-9) will provide widespread acceptance and affordability of XR applications in ISE. A deeper understanding of that progression will indicate the emergence of a new teaching and training paradigm within ISE. It will also reduce the gap between conceptual understanding and practical implementation which is prevalent within ISE. Hence, the aim of this study is to comprehend the TRLs of XR applications within ISE. For this, a systematic review of literature in the Association for Information Systems - eLibrary database was conducted on the articles published between 2014 and 2024 using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) method. A total set of 114 articles was coded into a spreadsheet and subsequently analysed using the spreadsheet slicer functionality. The outcome of the analysis shed insights into the type of XR applications used in IS Education, their TRLs, distribution of articles over time, research methods and the theoretical foundation of studies. The preliminary results reveal that VR applications are widely used in IS Education with TRL- 2 followed by TRLs 4 and 1. The distribution of articles saw a steady progression in recent years. Whereas systematic literature review was a predominant method used in many articles to understand the implications of XR applications in ISE. Due to the rapid advancement in spatial computing and the emergence of the metaverse, periodic reviews will be essential for a comprehensive understanding of TRLs of ISE applications.

articleTitle: Virtual Labs for Mechanical dynamics – a distraction OR a catalyst for better learning
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: This paper discusses the inclusion of a series of virtual laboratories into a second-year mechanical dynamics class. The goal was to explore if these virtual laboratories could improve the motivation levels of the student cohort and also enhance the learning and understanding outcomes of the students. Traditional teaching methods present mechanisms as static two-dimensional sketches, limiting students' ability to visualize motion and connect theoretical analyses to physical responses. By integrating a Simulation Based Learning (SBL) component, the study aims to assess whether such interactive virtual laboratories impact students' ability to understand the subject matter and their motivation to learn. The approach considered includes a MATLAB®, Simulink® and Simscape™ Multibody™ based mini project designed to deepen students' understanding of dynamics through problem-solving, analytical solutions verification, and the use of numerical methods for complex problems.

articleTitle: Peace Engineering - New Mexico Dashboard Case Study
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: Peace Engineering is the application of STEAM principles, sustainable practices, cultural sensitivity, and innovation to promote and support peace. It recognizes the important contribution that engineering, the sciences (social and physical), and other disciplines such as law and finance, working together, make toward a world where prosperity, sustainability, security, transparency, and diplomacy, and where a culture of equity and quality thrive. As an outcome of the WEEF-GEDC 2018 Global Peace Engineering conference, the University of New Mexico School of Engineering created an undergraduate minor in Peace Engineering comprising 15 hours of coursework, open to all disciplines, to collaboratively address global challenges and to educate “street smart” professionals of all disciplines. A principal goal and tool for Peace Engineering is verifiable trusted data, essential for making decisions. The Dashboard presented in this paper is the outcome of a final project of the ENG 220 (Engineering, Business, Sustainability, Ethics, Society, and Justice, Equity, Diversity, Accessibility, Inclusion) class in the Peace Engineering Minor program at UNM. Fifty-four undergraduate students participated, with 6 teams working in Water, and 4 in Air Quality, Health, and Finance/Economics. The Dashboard is an ongoing project that provides verifiable trusted data to community members and decision makers.

articleTitle: Fighting the gender drop off from STEM careers throughout the University-Industry Collaboration: Effects of Corporate Mentorship
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: The number of women in STEM careers has historically been low compared to the number of men enrolled. This is due to cultural causes, customs and stigmatization of engineering professionals. In the best cases, between 14-20% of women have been found in STEM careers at university. A private university in Mexico, committed to gender equity, has tried through different strategies to increase the number of women in STEM careers. One of these strategies is an initiative called Ingenia (Women in Engineering and Sciences) that includes actions focused on integral development, prevention of discrimination, among others.A notable effort by Ingenia Women in Engineering and Sciences to increase the participation and retention of women in STEM fields consists of organizing mentoring sessions in which executives from various corporations act as mentors for female students from this university pursuing careers in STEM fields. In this report we analyze the impact of having direct contact with high-level managers (CEOs and high direction managers) of training partners as mentors for female students studying engineering. During the mentoring sessions, the experts share their experiences and achievements and the obstacles they have had to overcome to reach their place today. For this research, a qualitative method was used, with a sample of 210 female engineering students participating in the mentoring sessions.The results indicate that through personalized interaction they can not only take their mentor as a role model but also motivate their professional path to have this interaction. Much of the success of this initiative is contact and personal reflection with women already in leader positions in industry. Additionally, the students who carried out the experience with managers of training partner companies declared greater strength in their performance and in their career as STEM students. Data analysis revealed that 83.4% of the students reinforced their decision to be part of STEM careers and 88.9% found the advice of successful people within companies motivating. Additionally, the comments among the students were very supportive of each other and asked for interaction with other mentors. Our results clearly indicate that personalized reflection helps to understand the problems of the unfavorable environment for women within STEM careers and helps reduce career desertion.

articleTitle: Integrating Real-World Challenges and Social Impact into Engineering Education for Advancing Sustainable Development Goals
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: One of the main goals at our university is human flourishing which we define as the path each person follows to become a better version of themselves. It includes a sense of purpose and commitment to leave the world better than we found it. Our university is dedicated to advancing the sustainable development of our society. A key element is to educate professionals conscious about the global challenges and motivated to improve their context utilizing their disciplinary knowledge and skills to address the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). The purpose of this study is to identify and quantify the compulsory engineering courses that formally address SDGs and engage students in applying their disciplinary competencies in real-world contexts, resulting in positive social impact. Mapping these efforts will enable the measurement of their impact and the recognition of initial outcomes. This study presents an approach of formal integration of social perspective in the engineering curriculum of our engineering programs and analyses its impact in terms of students involved, number of courses, SDGs addressed per course, collaboration with Educational Partners, and some examples of the implemented challenges. 20,000 undergraduate engineering students distributed in 18 engineering programs participate in compulsory courses with humanistic outlook along their studies. Overall, 120 courses are dedicated to addressing challenges with social impact. All 17 SDGs are included in these courses, generating challenges and reflection processes in the students. Through these experiences, our students discover their potential to be change agents in the exercise of their profession.

articleTitle: Aligning Students’ Foreknowledge: A Practice Report From Third Year Elective "Laser Technology"
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: Based on their individual diverse educational background students enter undergraduate programs with highly different foreknowledge. Experience shows that the degree of difference can be challenging for lecturers as well as students. This paper discusses a crash course approach to align the foreknowledge needed by students to thrive in the actual course content. As the discussed crash course was not delivered as a pre-course but uses lecture time of the actual course instead, possible advantages and disadvantages for course planning and implementation, and the student’s development are discussed. In result, at the beginning of the third-year elective "Laser Technology for Engineers" high differences in the needed foreknowledge could be observed across the participating N = 26 undergrad engineering students. Hierarchical regression models identified the UEQ GPA and the number of STEM related advanced courses for UEQ as two significant predictors. This significant predictor property disappears after participating in the three-weeks crash-course to align the students’ foreknowledge.
