Alternative predictors, i.e., conscientiousness, current undergraduate program GPA, and performance in foreknowledge test, also did not show any predictor property, giving strong support that the students benefited from the crash course approach as observed differences in foreknowledge could be compensated.

articleTitle: Professional Skills – A Cross Cultural Perspective
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: Practitioners, accrediting bodies, academics, and students all agree that a well-rounded engineer must have a mix of professional and technical skills to effectively contribute to their roles and society at large. Professional skills have an important role to play in graduate employment and career development. Studies have pointed out that recent graduates have generally not developed the professional skills required, identifying some of the challenges engineering programs face in meeting industry expectations with regards to students’ professional skills. This paper is based on preliminary findings from a research project investigating professional skill development and assessment in engineering programs. It specifically reports on a subset of the data from different international contexts, discussing the perspective of academics working in some of the top universities in India and Australia, identifying areas for future collaboration.

articleTitle: Accelerating Learning with AI: Improving Students’ Capability to Receive and Build Automated Feedback for Programming Courses
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) based tutoring assistance has shown great potential in delivering adaptive and personalized education. The programming subjects, boasting a large on-campus student body and an active online presence via discussion boards, are well-suited for evaluating the accessibility, engagement, and satisfaction of GenAI-based tutoring assistance. In this paper, we explore the pros and cons of a GenAI-based feedback system, specifically fine-tuning a Large Language Model (LLM), as a potential tool for providing personalized programming subject matter expertise and guiding students towards solutions with interpretability and visualization. To better address the technical issues students encounter in programming and ensure our model provides accurate and professional debugging solutions, we further develop a visualized interaction tool for code interpretation and prompts optimization. Additionally, this paper compares the effectiveness of online discussion boards and the developed LLM in assisting students’ questions and personalized support.

articleTitle: Mitigating Digital Distractions in Higher Education: An Empirical Study on Awareness and Intervention Strategies
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: Digital distractions present a significant challenge in higher education, impacting students’ academic performance and ability to focus. This study explores methods to reduce digital distractions and improve academic performance by understanding the sources of these distractions and implementing strategies to raise awareness and foster self-regulation among students. The focus is specifically on students in engineering disciplines, including Aerospace Engineering, Mechanical Engineering, and Electronic Engineering at ETSID UPV. By enhancing "learn to learn" competencies, this research aims to develop critical competencies for managing distractions.

articleTitle: Literature Review Paper: Exploring Engineering Students Perceptions of Engineering Accreditation
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: Students pursue engineering for various reasons, for example, making money, helping others, inventing or designing things, and developing new knowledge and skills. Many of the very professionals engineering students strive to become, are members of the professional societies that develop criteria and set the standards for engineering program accreditation. Accreditation commissioners comprise professional societies that make final decisions and guide program evaluations. The developed criteria are shared with engineering departments and faculty to prepare for upcoming reviews. The interaction between engineering departments and ABET is reciprocal, as departments receive criteria from ABET and must demonstrate that they satisfy the criteria for accreditation. However, students are often on the periphery of this relationship, despite being directly impacted by the criteria. This hierarchical relationship creates a disconnect between students and the accreditation of engineering programs. Despite ABET's pivotal role in shaping engineering education and its emphasis on ensuring graduates meet global workforce standards, students generally lack awareness of ABET's objectives. Considering ABET's mission to enhance the quality of education, there is a need for a student-centered approach to accreditation. This literature review aims to explore the literature on students’ perspectives of ABET in existing literature, where ABET is primarily discussed in the context of faculty and program implementation of criteria. This systematized literature review follows a sequential procedure. To ensure a broad search, engineering, and education databases were selected to search for relevant articles on past and current research around ABET student outcomes. Searching the various databases with specific keywords identified 1,054 articles, which were then screened based on inclusion criteria to determine their eligibility for the review. The final 30 articles were closely reviewed and synthesized to explore students' perspectives on ABET accreditation, student learning outcomes, and the integration of ABET criteria in engineering education. Three themes emerged from the synthesis and review process: 1) Active Student Engagement and Agency; 2) Assessment of Student Learning Outcomes; and 3) Perceptions and Attitudes of Engineering Students. Active student engagement and agency emerge as crucial factors in deepening understanding of engineering concepts and fostering essential skills for professional practice. Assessment practices must evolve to effectively gauge student achievement in alignment with ABET standards, especially in project-based courses where traditional methods may fall short. Comprehending students' perceptions and attitudes towards ABET accreditation is vital for informing curriculum development and accreditation processes. By incorporating students' perspectives, educators and stakeholders can better align engineering education with industry demands and enhance students' preparedness for the workforce. This literature review offers valuable insights into the limited documentation of students' viewpoints on ABET. The findings highlighted the absence of students' perspectives on ABET accreditation. They emphasized the importance of further investigating engineering students' perceptions of accreditation, and how ABET student outcomes criteria can be leveraged to align with students' future goals.

articleTitle: Overcoming Transfer Shock Across Educational Institutions: From Technologist To Engineer
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: The global shortage of engineering scarce skills, particularly for complex problem solving, has incentivized the transfer of qualified technicians and technologists (from technical/applied institutions) to traditional universities offering bachelor’s in engineering programmes. This paper investigates the receptiveness of the transfer culture of a traditional university in South Africa, to which technicians and technologists transfer. The objective of this exploratory study is to lay the groundwork for a more holistic and successful transfer experience from a practical or applied sciences context (University of Technology - UoT) to a traditional, research-intensive university environment. Existing research speaks of "transfer shock", which can be overcome by creating a transfer-receptive culture, including institutional, academic and social perspectives. The research question is: How can receiving institutions better support UoT transfer students? A mixed-method survey was used to gain insights into the recent experiences of transfer students, focusing on the institutional (systemic), academic (cognitive-affective) and social (affective) support mechanisms (or lack thereof), as indicators of the receptiveness of the transfer culture of the receiving institution. Survey data indicates that most transferring students experienced transfer shock, exacerbated by support infrastructure typically not tailored to an increasingly culturally and socioeconomically diverse student body. Many respondents indicated that they experienced academic inadequacy or "impostor syndrome" after transferring. This exploratory study serves to illuminate what is becoming a global phenomenon of increasingly diverse student bodies in higher education environments, and graduates in workplaces.

articleTitle: Engineering Assessment in the Age of Generative Artificial Intelligence: A Critical Analysis
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has significantly impacted higher education, offering numerous benefits alongside notable risks, particularly concerning academic integrity. This paper reviews the assessment landscape in the context of GenAI and critically analyses a key GenAI assessment framework against the latest assessment integrity research in engineering. Our analysis indicates that this framework presents a valuable opportunity for advancing engineering education.

articleTitle: Fostering Belonging: The Impact of a Wise Intervention on Diverse Engineering Students
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: This study investigates the impact of a scalable, online intervention, that includes sense of belonging and growth mindset activities, on first-year engineering students at a South African research-intensive institution, focusing on those from historically underrepresented groups, including first-generation students and those who come from a less advantaged socioeconomic status (SES) background. The intervention, based on the difference-education approach, aims to foster a sense of belonging, improve academic performance, and promote equity. Participants engaged in activities such as watching videos of diverse senior students sharing their experiences, completing reflections, and surveys. Data was collected from first-year engineering students in 2023 and 2024, and included participants' sense of belonging, emotional experiences, and academic performance in a gateway mathematics course. Statistical analyses revealed that all participants felt a sense of belonging, with first-generation and less advantaged SES students reporting significantly higher positive emotions compared to other students (p<0.05). Notably, intervention participants achieved significantly higher final marks in the engineering mathematics module than non-participants (p<0.05). Thematic analysis identified common themes and challenges faced by students from different backgrounds. The study also explored the synergistic effects of combining a sense of belonging intervention with a growth mindset intervention, revealing promising results for student retention and success. This research contributes to literature emphasizing the effectiveness of wise social belonging interventions in improving university performance and reducing achievement gaps in engineering education. The findings underscore the importance of addressing social belonging to promote diversity, equity, and inclusion in higher education and provide valuable insights for educators and administrators seeking to create more inclusive learning environments.

articleTitle: Collaborative Pathways: Enhancing Engineering Education through Industry-Academia Partnerships in Africa
publicationTitle: 2024 World Engineering Education Forum - Global Engineering Deans Council (WEEF-GEDC)
abstract: The development of Africa’s engineering education is crucial for addressing the continent’s infrastructure and technological challenges. This paper explores the role of Industry-Academia Partnerships (IAPs) in transforming engineering education across Africa. Through a comprehensive survey of universities, industry stakeholders, and students from various African regions, this study examines the current state of IAPs and their impact on skill development, curriculum relevance, and employability. The findings reveal that while IAPs hold immense potential to bridge the gap between theoretical knowledge and practical skills, significant challenges such as inadequate funding, poor institutional frameworks, and limited industry engagement persist. The study proposes a sustainable model for strengthening these partnerships, focusing on experiential learning, curriculum development, and collaborative research. The implementation of this model can enhance the quality of engineering graduates, foster innovation, and contribute to Africa’s socio-economic development. Recommendations are made for policies and strategies to overcome the barriers to effective IAPs, ensuring that engineering education aligns with the evolving demands of industry and society.
